title: Optics
tagline: How light travels, bends and interferes
summary: Geometrical optics of mirrors and lenses, then the wave theory: interference, diffraction and polarisation.
overview: Optics is the physics of light: how it travels, bends, reflects, interferes, spreads and carries a direction of oscillation. It is also the most precise measuring technology physics has. Interferometers compare lengths to a fraction of a wavelength, gratings and etalons separate spectral lines a thousandth of a nanometre apart, and the same principles design camera lenses, optical fibres and the largest telescopes.

The course starts with geometrical optics, in which light travels along rays. Fermat's principle gives the laws of reflection and refraction, and from them total internal reflection, optical fibres, image formation by lenses and mirrors (with a sign convention stated once and kept), ray-transfer matrices and the classical instruments. The remaining chapters use the wave theory, with light as the electromagnetic wave of the magnetism course: interference of two and of many beams, diffraction by slits, gratings and circular apertures, and finally polarisation, described with Jones vectors and matrices and explained at boundaries by the Fresnel equations.

The single idea to carry through the course is the optical path difference. Bright and dark fringes, thin-film colours, grating orders, the zeros of a diffraction pattern and the retardance of a wave plate are all statements about it, once any phase change of π on reflection has been counted. The small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ is used constantly and should be labelled each time; many apparent paradoxes are cases where it has quietly failed.
outcomes: Derive the laws of reflection and refraction from Fermat's principle, and apply Snell's law, total internal reflection and the numerical aperture of a fibre.
Locate images formed by spherical surfaces, thin lenses and mirrors with a consistent sign convention, and use the lensmaker's equation.
Analyse multi-element paraxial systems with ray-transfer matrices, and compute the magnification of a magnifier, microscope and telescope.
Explain coherence and coherence length, and calculate two-beam interference patterns for Young's slits, thin films and the Michelson interferometer.
Derive the Airy transmission function of a Fabry–Pérot interferometer and compute its finesse, free spectral range and resolving power.
Derive the Fraunhofer patterns of a single slit and of N slits, and use the grating equation and the resolving power mN.
Apply the Rayleigh criterion θ = 1.22λ/D to telescopes, cameras and the eye, and describe Fresnel diffraction with Fresnel zones.
Describe polarisation states and optical elements with Jones vectors and matrices, and apply Malus's law.
Derive the Fresnel equations and Brewster's angle from the electromagnetic boundary conditions, and compute reflectances.
Explain birefringence, wave plates and optical activity, and design a quarter-wave or half-wave plate.

chapters.title: Rays and images
chapters.summary: Fermat's principle, refraction and fibres, thin lenses and mirrors, ray matrices and instruments.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Coherence, Young's double slit, thin films, the Michelson and Fabry–Pérot interferometers.

chapters.title: Diffraction
chapters.summary: Single-slit and N-slit diffraction, gratings, the Rayleigh criterion, Fresnel zones and Fourier optics.

chapters.title: Polarisation
chapters.summary: Jones vectors, Malus's law, the Fresnel equations and Brewster's angle, wave plates and optical activity.

history.title: Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics
history.detail: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen), working in Cairo, completed his Book of Optics around 1021, arguing that vision is caused by light entering the eye and studying reflection and refraction by experiment.

history.title: The sine law of refraction
history.detail: Willebrord Snell found that the sines of the angles of incidence and refraction are in a constant ratio, but did not publish it. René Descartes published the law in La Dioptrique in 1637.

history.title: Fermat's principle of least time
history.detail: Pierre de Fermat derived the law of refraction from the principle that light takes the path of least time, which requires light to travel more slowly in denser media.

history.title: Huygens's wave theory
history.detail: Christiaan Huygens's Traité de la lumière explained reflection, refraction and the double refraction of Iceland spar by the propagation of secondary wavelets.

history.title: Newton's Opticks
history.detail: Isaac Newton's Opticks described his experiments on the prism and on the coloured rings of thin films, and argued for a particle theory of light.

history.title: Young's interference
history.detail: In lectures to the Royal Society from 1801 to 1803, Thomas Young explained the colours of thin films by the interference of waves, and his two-slit experiment measured the wavelength of light.

history.title: Polarisation by reflection
history.detail: Étienne-Louis Malus found that light reflected from glass is polarised, named the phenomenon, and stated the cos² law. David Brewster found the law tan θ_B = n in 1815.

history.title: Fresnel's memoir on diffraction
history.detail: Augustin-Jean Fresnel's memoir on diffraction won the French Academy's prize in 1819 after François Arago observed the bright spot in the shadow of a disc that Poisson had derived from it as an objection.

history.title: Fraunhofer's gratings
history.detail: Joseph von Fraunhofer described diffraction gratings and used them to measure the wavelengths of the dark lines in the solar spectrum.

history.title: Rayleigh's criterion
history.detail: Lord Rayleigh gave the criterion for the resolving power of optical instruments. Albert Michelson's interferometer followed in 1881, and Charles Fabry and Alfred Pérot described their multiple-beam interferometer in 1897–1899.

references.title: Optics
references.note: Fifth edition. The standard undergraduate text, from rays and matrices through interference, diffraction, polarisation and Fourier optics; the sign convention of this course is Hecht's.

references.title: Introduction to Optics
references.authors: Frank L. Pedrotti, Leno M. Pedrotti and Leno S. Pedrotti
references.note: Third edition. Clear and well organised, with especially good chapters on matrix methods, the Fabry–Pérot interferometer and Jones calculus.

references.title: Principles of Optics
references.note: Seventh edition. The classic advanced reference for the electromagnetic theory of optics, diffraction theory, aberrations and coherence.

references.title: Fundamentals of Photonics
references.authors: Bahaa E. A. Saleh and Malvin Carl Teich
references.note: Third edition. A modern treatment of Fourier optics, beam optics, fibres, polarisation and lasers, for going beyond the course.

references.title: University Physics
references.authors: Hugh D. Young and Roger A. Freedman
references.note: Fifteenth edition, the optics chapters, for a first pass and for many routine problems.

references.title: Introduction to Electrodynamics
references.note: Fourth edition, chapter 9, for the electromagnetic waves, boundary conditions and Fresnel equations behind the wave optics of this course.
